run.title: Strategic fit
run.objective: Decide whether a supply chain should be responsive or efficient by reading the uncertainty its own customer promise creates.
explainer: Performance improves when a company's supply chain strategy is aligned with its competitive strategy. Competitive strategy is the customer promise: which needs this firm will satisfy particularly well. A value-focused retailer like DMart promises low prices and dependable availability. A quick-commerce format promises convenience and speed, and its customers will pay a little more for immediate availability. Supply chain strategy is the answer to what the chain must therefore be good at — sourcing, where you manufacture, where inventory sits, how you transport and fulfil. When the two disagree, either customers are disappointed or costs rise sharply, or both.

The link between them is implied demand uncertainty, and it is the idea most worth slowing down on. It is not how variable demand is — it is the uncertainty the supply chain faces because of the promise it made. Shorter lead times, higher variety, more channels, higher service levels, and faster innovation all raise it. So a product with perfectly stable demand can still create high implied uncertainty if you promise it in two hours. Where implied uncertainty is high, forecast error is higher, stockouts and markdowns are likelier, and margins tend to be higher.

Matching them is the zone of strategic fit: high implied uncertainty is best served by responsiveness, low implied uncertainty by efficiency. Responsiveness costs more, because it is bought with buffer inventory, buffer capacity, faster transport, and stronger information systems. A firm not yet on the cost-responsiveness frontier can improve both at once; once on it, more responsiveness means more cost. Fit also has a scope — it strengthens as alignment widens from one function, to across functions, to across firms.

worked.setup: Marketing promises high variety with fast delivery. Distribution minimises its own cost by using slow transport and batching orders, and suppliers were chosen only on low price rather than reliability. Customers experience delays and poor availability.
worked.move: Read the promise first: short lead times and high variety both raise implied demand uncertainty, so this chain needs responsiveness. Then read what it is actually built for — slow transport, batching, and price-selected suppliers are efficiency choices, which suit low implied uncertainty. The fix is to rebuild distribution and supplier selection for the promised responsiveness, or to change the promise so it matches what the chain can do.
worked.because: Distribution is not being badly run here. Batching orders and buying on price are locally efficient and each function can defend its own numbers. The failure is that the chain is optimised for a different promise than the one marketing sold, which is exactly what a lack of fit looks like from the inside.

glossary.plain: The competitive strategy and the supply chain strategy targeting the same customer priorities.
The uncertainty the supply chain must absorb because of the promise it made, not just demand variation.
Being able to handle swings in quantity, short lead times, wide variety, and high service — at higher cost.
Delivering at the lowest possible cost, usually through standardisation, high utilisation, and stable operations.
The lowest cost achievable at each level of responsiveness; on it, more speed must be paid for.
The band where the chain's responsiveness matches the implied uncertainty the promise creates.
Being efficient where uncertainty is low and responsive where it is high, instead of one design for everything.

handoff.connects: Fit tells you what the chain must be good at. It does not tell you which levers set that — and those levers are the next lecture.

run.title: The six drivers of supply chain performance
run.objective: Name which driver a decision actually changes, and the second driver it forces to move with it.
explainer: Six drivers are the levers managers actually control: facilities, inventory, transportation, information, sourcing, and pricing. Together they set the balance between responsiveness and efficiency. They are not the only things that matter, but most other decisions — forecasting, scheduling, supplier contracts — sit under one of them. Facilities are the physical locations where product is produced, stored, or fulfilled. Inventory is everything in the chain: raw materials, work in progress, finished goods. Transportation is the movement between points.

The remaining three are the ones students under-weight. Information is data and analysis about demand, inventory, facilities, cost, and customers, and it is often the biggest driver because it improves every other one. Sourcing is the choice of who performs an activity — make or buy, in-house or outsourced, domestic or global. Pricing is a supply chain driver, not only a marketing decision, because it shapes when demand arrives: pricing express delivery higher sorts customers by what they value, and a promotion is a supply chain event that changes volumes and replenishment needs.

The point of the framework is that the drivers interact, so a decision on one usually forces a change in at least one other. Add facilities closer to customers and transportation may fall while facility cost and total inventory rise. Cut inventory hard and working capital improves, but lost sales rise unless transport and information can replenish faster. There is no best combination — the right one depends on the competitive strategy and the uncertainty being faced.

worked.setup: A quick-commerce firm promises very fast delivery. It does this by positioning inventory in small fulfilment points close to customers rather than serving the country from one or two centralised warehouses.
worked.move: Name the driver being changed: this is a facilities decision, and it drags inventory along with it. Responsiveness rises because stock is near the customer. Fixed facility cost rises. Total inventory in the system usually rises too, because the same demand is now covered from many small points instead of one pooled location.
worked.because: The tempting reading is that more facilities is simply better. More facilities usually do improve responsiveness, but they also increase fixed costs and often increase total inventory — so whether it is better depends on what these customers value and are willing to pay for.

run.stem: Build the reasoning chain. All three steps must agree before the conclusion is secure.

steps.label: Step 1 · Diagnose the first decision
options: Strategic fit: Recognise a facilities-and-inventory choice that raises responsiveness while raising fixed cost, since one driver never delivers fit by itself.
Strategic fit: Keep both strategies unchanged, because each function is already locally efficient on its own budget and targets.
Strategic fit: Measure suppliers only on unit purchase price and ignore availability, because the lowest landed cost defines a fit supply chain.
Strategic fit: Redesign the chain for the promised responsiveness or change the promise, because performance always fails when the two diverge.
